original_question: Is the class of linear lattices a variety, meaning a class definable by a set of equations?
target_in_paper: Section 2 ("Problems of 2025"), Problem 35: "Is the class of linear lattices a variety? (That is, is it definable by a set of equations.)"
correct_elements: Your draft captures the paper's target essentially verbatim. It asks exactly about whether the class of linear lattices is a variety, and it already includes the paper's own gloss that this means being definable by equations. This is the precise open problem recorded as Problem 35.
missing_details: The paper does not locally define "linear lattice"; to make the question stand-alone, one should say that a linear lattice is a lattice isomorphic to a lattice of commuting equivalence relations on some set.
If one wants full self-containment, "definable by a set of equations" should be read as an equational class of lattices, i.e. axiomatizable by lattice identities.
The quantifier is over the whole class of linear lattices; the paper does not restrict to finite, complemented, modular, or Arguesian lattices.
The paper presents this as an open problem, not as a conjecture or theorem, and gives no sharper nearby reformulation than the parenthetical explanation of "variety."
No ambient ring/field, degree restriction, homogeneity assumption, nilpotency condition, or asymptotic phrase such as "for all sufficiently large m" is involved here.
refined_question: Is the class of all linear lattices—that is, all lattices isomorphic to lattices of commuting equivalence relations on some set—an equational class of lattices (equivalently, a variety)?
justification: The exact target in arXiv:2509.25446 is Problem 35 in Section 2. The neighboring items are different questions about the same notion—Problem 34 asks about self-duality, while Problem 36 asks whether lattices satisfying all orders of the Arguesian law can fail to be linear—so the sharp paper-faithful choice is to keep the focus on Problem 35 alone. The only substantive addition needed for a stand-alone formulation is to spell out the standard meaning of "linear lattice," since the notebook itself only states the problem and cites Jónsson's paper.
